blocks.html_en: 4.4 Live-Streamed Videos

sentences.en: 4.4 Live-Streamed Videos

blocks.html_en: Live streaming is increasingly adopted by developers to increase visibility, support education, and foster community engagement, as noted in Kokinda and Rodeghero (2023). Such data enable unobtrusive observation of behaviors in natural settings, helping reduce observer bias (Mahtani et al. 2018). Despite this potential, live streaming remains underexplored in software-engineering research. Progress has been made by curating and labeling live-streamed videos and by developing the observer-dev.online platform for software-engineering researchers as created by Alaboudi (2023). From this dataset, we used all 15 curated videos (total duration: 36:01:30) and conducted a thematic analysis, with both the dataset and our qualitative findings made publicly available (Chou 2026b). Since little is known about why and how developers insert log statements, we relied on the segmentation of each video into debugging episodes (e.g., “Testing the program and reading the outputs”, “Interacting with a file of code (Edit)”) provided in Alaboudi and LaToza (2023). These segments allowed us to efficiently identify moments when developers began adding log statements to source code.

blocks.html_en: Validation

sentences.en: Validation

blocks.html_en: Because our dataset is derived from simply removed logging statements, there is the potential risk that some collected cases may be core-functionality-based logging — not specifically ad-hoc logs used for runtime comprehension. For example, developers may remove print statements that were originally intended for user-facing output or other purposes. To account for this possibility, we sought to assess the reliability of two options for log curation: one option that is this looser removal-only scheme, and one option that is stricter, which requires more explicit knowledge of developer intention of some debugging or comprehension activity. We anticipate a precision–coverage tradeoff between the two: the looser scheme might admit more false positives, whereas the stricter scheme might exclude valid ad-hoc logs. Specifically, the looser matching scheme identifies commit messages that contain both a removal-related verb and a noun referring to a common debugging statement, such as console.log or print. The stricter one requires a removal-related verb, an adjective indicating debugging or accidental intent, and a noun describing the removed statement. This stricter pattern is intended to capture commit messages such as “remove accidental print statements” or “delete debugging console.log.” The complete regular expressions are provided in the replication package.

blocks.html_en: The initial qualitative coding phase began with the first author reviewing five videos, identifying 45 ad-hoc logs, and developing an initial codebook, which is provided in the replication package at Chou (2026b). The second author then independently coded the same set of videos using this codebook. Inter-rater reliability between the two coders was high (Cohen’s \(\kappa = 0.849\)). Any disagreements or uncertainties were subsequently resolved through team discussions during weekly meetings until consensus was reached. After this calibration process, first author then proceeded with coding the remaining dataset. In total, fifteen videos from Alaboudi and LaToza (2023), amounting to more than 36 hours of material, were analyzed, resulting in the identification of 92 ad-hoc logs. Videos were labeled sequentially from V1 to V15. Three videos contained no ad-hoc logs: V5 and V6 (Rust) relied solely on compile-time error logs, while V14 (CSharp) consistently used the Visual Studio debugger.

blocks.html_en: Figures 4 and 5 show where developers placed ad-hoc logs across JavaScript, Java, and Python. The largest share appears in function-type blocks in all three languages in both stricter and looser datasets: 77.1% (L) and 74.4% (S) in JavaScript, 50.7% (L) and 45.1% (S) in Java, and 41.0% (L) and 43.1% (S) in Python. By “function-type block,” we mean that the log statement resides directly in the body of a function or method, rather than nested within a conditional, loop, or error-handling block. This distinction separates, for example, a console.log at the top of a function from one placed inside an if branch or a try block. Because the language datasets differ in collection window, event sampling, extraction and filtering, and validation precision (Sections 4 and 5.1), their absolute percentages should not be compared as estimates of language effects. We use them to characterize placement patterns within each language. If-else placements are the next largest group: 15.0% (L) and 18.0% (S) in JavaScript, 24.8% (L) and 31.3% (S) in Java, and 30.3% (L) and 29.9% (S) in Python. Error-handling blocks are a minority in the ad-hoc-log samples. For example, JavaScript TryStatement and CatchClause placements together account for less than 4% in both L and S.

blocks.html_en: These patterns differ from Li et al. (2020)’s findings on production logs, which showed that logging statements are commonly placed in error-handling and conditional blocks. Li et al. (2020) focused on industrial Java systems, whereas our dataset is primarily drawn from open-source projects across multiple languages. To support a like-for-like comparison, we also collected production logs from the same repositories using the procedure described in §4.2 and examined their surrounding block types, as shown in Fig. 6. Our production-log sample is broadly consistent with prior work: production logs are more concentrated in catch/except-like blocks and if–else branches. For example, in our JavaScript production-log sample, CatchClause accounts for 15.25% of logging statements and IfStatement accounts for 36.28%, compared with 1.2% and 15.0%, respectively, in the JavaScript L sample. Java shows the same pattern: production logs are concentrated in CatchClause (21.49%) and IfStmt (36.98%), with an additional 7.02% appearing in TryStmt. Ad-hoc logs are less frequent in these locations and are more often placed directly in function or method bodies.

blocks.html_en: For each Java source file, the analyzer examined the first top-level type declared in that file. We classified that type as a “concurrency-type class” when its declaration directly extended a recognized concurrency-related class (e.g., Thread) or directly implemented a recognized concurrency-related interface (e.g., Runnable). blocks.html_en: Across languages, we observed from two perspectives: (i) the names of functions or methods themselves where ad-hoc logs are present, and (ii) in JavaScript specifically, the names of functions that accept callbacks containing ad-hoc logs. When considering functions and methods directly, we find that each ecosystem reflects its dominant paradigm. In JavaScript, ad-hoc logs are concentrated in lifecycle methods such as render, constructor, componentDidMount, and ngOnInit, pointing to the prevalence of logging in frontend component initialization and update flows. In Java, the most frequent names include main, run, and execute, which correspond to entry points and execution control, but also testing and GUI-related names such as test_0, test_alter_first, and actionPerformed. In Python, the top names are more generic, reflecting its use across diverse domains: common lifecycle functions (__init__, __call__), general execution (main, run, update), and some workload-specific routines, for example in machine learning (forward, train) and developer tooling (_lint_html_files). Unlike Java and JavaScript, no single pattern dominates beyond the natural diversity of Python applications. Meanwhile, in JavaScript’s callback-accepting functions, the most common names are then, catch, and on, highlighting asynchronous and event-driven control. Taken together, these distributions suggest that ad-hoc logs appear where developers most often need to reason about complex, framework-controlled behaviors: lifecycle timing in JavaScript UIs, concurrency and control flow in Java, and a wide range of tasks shaped by Python’s flexibility across domains.

Comparing cyclomatic complexity across datasets, we found that logged functions are consistently more complex. In JavaScript (BigQuery and GitHub Archive), logged functions had higher mean and median complexity than all functions (BigQuery: \(\mu =7.77\), \(\tilde{x}=4.0\) vs. \(\mu =3.32\), \(\tilde{x}=2.0\); GitHub: \(\mu =5.62\), \(\tilde{x}=3.0\) vs. \(\mu =3.64\), \(\tilde{x}=2.0\)), with \(p<0.001\) in both cases. Consistent with prior findings (Jiang et al. 2023), developers often add labels to help trace logged variables back to their origins in the console output. Our analysis shows that when a log includes two arguments, 84.7% in JS and 76.8% in PY contain at least one literal. (We excluded Java from this analysis since only 0.6% of print statements have two arguments.) Among these, 51.5% (JS) and 38.8% (PY) explicitly reference the other argument within the literal. For example, in console.log(‘Results: ’, results), the string label “Results: ” clarifies the meaning of the logged variable value, making it easier to locate in the output stream.

blocks.html_en: Table 6 presents the top 10 most frequent literal contents in ad-hoc logs for each programming language. The symbol R denotes a sequence of characters repeated more than three times; for example, =R represents repeated equal signs such as “====,” often used to create separation markers or to highlight certain content in the log output. The most dominant entries across the three languages are template-like strings, which often serve as lightweight markers in logs. Strings such as here, clicked, and hi are frequently used to indicate control-flow checkpoints or event triggers during execution. In the case of Java, transaction-related lifecycle markers (e.g., Transaction started, Transaction committed) are prevalent, reinforcing our observation in Finding 1B.

sentences.en: 6.3 RQ3: Why do Developers Rely on Ad-Hoc Logs?

blocks.html_en: To answer RQ3 and RQ4, we shifted our focus to live-streamed data to address more qualitative questions and gain insight into why and how developers use ad-hoc logs. From analyzing and coding 15 live-stream videos and 92 obtained ad-hoc logs, we summarize our key findings as follows:

blocks.html_en: Understanding Program States (n=68)

sentences.en: Understanding Program States (n=68)

blocks.html_en: Developers often use ad-hoc logs to observe or compare program states for several reasons. A common reason is to capture states that are not immediately clear from the source code, such as states introduced by a third-party library or fetched via a web API. For example, the developer in V3 expressed uncertainty about a library function call’s effect and logged a boolean value triggered by a GUI click event, noting, “Does it return true when option changes, or does it return true when it set it on? That’s the thing I don’t know. Let’s find it out.” Developers also log multiple states to cross-reference their values, ensuring they align with expectations. For instance, the developer in V13 checked three boolean values with logs to iteratively verify they matched expectations. In other cases, logs are used to check the state of a single variable or condition, providing quick feedback on specific program values. To understand the initial program states when debugging the function, developers also inserted the logs right after the function to inspect the parameters. For example, the developer in V9 logged the parameter right after the function to check how the function works, “alright, let’s see what this does.” Developers also crafted their own formatting function when dealing with complex or non-readable program states. For example, the developer in V4 working on the curl project introduced a function what2name to transform a constant integer to a string, which increased the readability of logging outputs.

blocks.html_en: Iterations (n=27)

blocks.html_en: Developers progressively refined their logs to better understand program states and identify optimal logging points or variables. For instance, V15 revised the same log three times, evolving from console.log(this.props) to console.log(this.props.navigation.action) across multiple edit–run cycles. Likewise, V7 made six adjustments while tracing the call stack of a double-click event, moving the log back one level each time, and explained, “I don’t remember how all this works, so we are just gonna print to make sense of it.”

blocks.html_en: Varied Timing of Ad-hoc Log Removal

sentences.en: Varied Timing of Ad-hoc Log Removal

blocks.html_en: As anticipated, most ad-hoc logs were discarded once they fulfilled their immediate purpose. Specifically, many logs were deleted right after their output was inspected (n=61), and most were observed or confirmed to have been eventually removed (n=80). For the remaining cases, some logs could not be confirmed because the recordings ended before their fate was observed (n=7), while others were ultimately committed to the repository (n=5). Among the committed logs, three were intentionally retained as they evolved into production code (n=3), and two appeared to be accidental commits (n=2). Noteworthy instances include V1 storing logs in a git stash for potential reuse during future debugging, and V13 being prompted to remove a log immediately after viewing its output in the terminal.

blocks.html_en: Varied Strategies for Ad-Hoc Log Removal

sentences.en: Varied Strategies for Ad-Hoc Log Removal

blocks.html_en: The strategies employed for ad-hoc log removal were diverse. While direct deletion was the predominant approach (n=54), several alternative practices were observed. For example, V1 avoided committing files containing logs (n=2), and V9 temporarily commented out one log to facilitate run-to-run comparisons (n=2). In V13’s case, a linter tool prompted the removal of ad-hoc logs (n=1), and the developer also created and used an external environment (CodeSandbox) to capture debugging outputs in real time without altering the main codebase (n=3). However, not all log management actions were deliberate—V15 inadvertently committed two ad-hoc logs after forgetting to delete them (n=2).

blocks.html_en: 7.1 Perils and Promises of Learning from Mistakes

sentences.en: 7.1 Perils and Promises of Learning from Mistakes

blocks.html_en: As Henry Lieberman noted in (Lieberman 1997), “debugging is the dirty little secret of computer science.” This “dirt” has only accumulated over time, with using debuggers to understand runtime behavior often being regarded as the default solution, leading some developers to feel ambivalent or even reluctant to admit their use of “printf debugging” techniques (Beller et al. 2018). Such hesitation limits the research community’s insight into debugging behaviors, like ad-hoc print statement usage, which play a significant role in shaping final patches or feature development. Our research uncovers this “dirt,” through mining developers’ mistakes to offer the community new possibilities to understand ad-hoc logging practices.

blocks.html_en: Alaboudi and Latoza (2021) conducted analysis of live-streaming data and highlighted that software development is an iterative process involving frequent edit-run cycles. However, these small cycles are often hidden within local development environments, limiting the feasibility of large-scale studies. Previous research has addressed this challenge by either conducting costly lab studies (Gilmore 1991), analyzing live-streaming videos (Alaboudi and Latoza 2019), or requiring developers to install intrusive IDE plugins (Aniche et al. 2022; Beller et al. 2018). Our method opens new possibilities for scalable insights into these cycles.

blocks.html_en: While our collection of ad-hoc logs from revision-control systems enables large-scale analysis, there are limitations: (1) the mined data provides only a snapshot of logs unintentionally committed to version control, making it difficult to observe iterations in the log-authoring process; (2) although the surrounding source code offers some context, it does not capture the developers’ rationale for adding, removing, or evaluating the utility of these logs. To gain deeper insight into the context, reasoning, creation, and deletion of these logs, we mined and analyzed the live-streaming data.

blocks.html_en: Moreover, the distribution of the repository reveals that our dataset, similar to the repositories reported in Kalliamvakou et al. (2014), is skewed toward smaller, personal, and often inactive repositories. We chose not to explicitly exclude personal projects, as this distribution presents a double-edged sword for our analysis. Whereas large, well-maintained open-source projects often enforce linter checks on pull requests to prevent ad-hoc logs, as suggested by Foundation (2025), personal projects—wherein maintainers might carelessly push ad-hoc logs—allowed us to perform large-scale analysis. Future researchers using our dataset or similar methods should proceed with caution, as data without fine-grained filtering may not fully generalize to expert developers or contributors in collaborative open-source projects.

blocks.html_en: 7.2 Markers in the Forest of Complex Software Execution

sentences.en: 7.2 Markers in the Forest of Complex Software Execution

blocks.html_en: Each logging statement placed by developers can be understood as a marker left within the forest of execution, intended to make sense of code that would otherwise be difficult to navigate. Our analysis shows that ad-hoc logs are frequently inserted into threading-related code, asynchronous functions, callbacks, and the lifecycle methods of third-party libraries (Finding 1B). These contexts complicate reasoning because the order and timing of execution are often outside the developer’s immediate control. Logs in such locations serve as reference points for reconstructing runtime behavior. In addition, functions containing removed ad-hoc logs had higher observed cyclomatic complexity than the sampled function populations across all three languages (Finding 1C). This association is consistent with developers using logs in code that is structurally difficult to reason about, although the similar pattern among production logs indicates that it is not unique to ad-hoc logging.

blocks.html_en: While these findings may appear intuitive, the patterns of where developers place logs provide an opportunity to re-examine how software complexity is measured. The debate over which metrics—Cyclomatic Complexity, Cognitive Complexity, or custom alternatives—best capture developer-perceived difficulty has persisted for decades, such as discussion in Shepperd (1988); Scalabrino et al. (2017). Since controlled human studies remain expensive and difficult to scale, our dataset offers a complementary empirical lens and motivates future work examining whether logging behavior can complement established measures of code complexity and developer-perceived difficulty. This opens the door for future work to validate or refine existing metrics, or to propose new ones grounded in observed developer practices. In applied contexts, educators and maintainers could also use patterns of ad-hoc logging as a proxy for identifying code that is unusually challenging, helping to target refactoring efforts or calibrate the level of instructional material. For instance, the high frequency of logs used to understand React component lifecycles in JavaScript may point to aspects of the API design that warrant reconsideration or a separate visualization to support comprehension.

blocks.html_en: A single marker is rarely enough to navigate complex execution paths. As shown in Finding 4, developers often placed logs iteratively, refining their placement until the information was sufficient to understand program states and flows. This iterative pattern indicates that initial logs are frequently suboptimal for comprehension, functioning more as tentative probes than definitive solutions. These observations highlight an opportunity for future research: by building on insights from production log studies, it may be possible to recommend more effective initial logging locations such as techniques introduced in Fu et al. (2014); Li et al. (2020) and variables like (Liu et al. 2021). Such guidance could reduce the trial-and-error effort developers currently expend, allowing them to converge on useful runtime insights more quickly.

blocks.html_en: Effective logging is not only about where statements are placed, but also about the richness of the information they convey. Finding 2 shows that many ad-hoc logs extend beyond a simple message: developers often include labels, formatting strings, or custom debug helpers. Finding 3 further shows that developers craft anchor strings and selectively structure complex objects so that logs can be compared across states and used to trace execution over time. Together, these findings suggest that developers treat ad-hoc logs as deliberate reasoning aids rather than arbitrary print statements. This observation has direct implications for tool design. IDE support should not only recommend where to insert logs, but also help developers generate informative logs by suggesting discriminative anchor strings, relevant variable groupings, and readable object summaries tailored to the local context. Such support could be especially valuable in asynchronous or callback-heavy code, where developers must mentally map console output back to source locations and execution order. Our findings also suggest practical logging guidelines: developers benefit from logs that include stable textual anchors, explicit state summaries, and enough contextual detail to distinguish nearby execution points. Existing tools such as Log-it Jiang et al. (2023) begin to reduce the burden of connecting output to code, while prior work on visualization (Turcotte et al. 2022) and logging recommendation (Li 2020) points to promising directions for operationalizing these insights in future developer-support tools.

blocks.html_en: 7.4.1 Internal Threats to Validity

blocks.html_en: For the mined ad-hoc logs, a key internal threat is that some logs classified as ad-hoc may actually be removed production logs, which could affect the accuracy of our findings. To address this, we manually labeled 100 sample commits for each language and found that only a small portion were not used in an ad-hoc manner. In coding the live-streaming data, researcher bias is a common concern due to the subjective nature of qualitative analysis. We mitigated this by involving a second researcher and holding iterative discussions to minimize uncertainty and resolve any disagreements.

blocks.html_en: Our findings may not generalize to other programming languages or development contexts. Although our repository analysis covers Java, JavaScript, and Python, the qualitative analysis includes live-stream videos spanning a broader set of languages, and the two datasets should therefore not be interpreted as directly comparable language samples. The live-stream analysis is also based on a relatively small sample and may be subject to performance bias, as developers may behave differently while streaming their work as noted in Alaboudi and Latoza (2019). Moreover, the repositories represented in these videos are skewed toward personal or inactive projects, which may not reflect development practices in actively maintained or industrial projects. While the selection and representativeness of these videos were discussed by Alaboudi and Latoza (2019), our study uses them to investigate different research questions and therefore inherits additional limitations specific to our analysis. These factors limit the generalizability of our qualitative observations, which should be interpreted as exploratory evidence of how developers use ad-hoc logs rather than as representative estimates of broader developer behavior.

sentences.en: 8 Conclusion

blocks.html_en: This paper presented the first large-scale empirical study of ad-hoc, or “printf-style,” logging by systematically mining accidental commits and analyzing live-streamed programming sessions. By leveraging over 800,000 removed log statements across JavaScript, Java, and Python, as well as 36 hours of qualitative observations, we demonstrated that ad-hoc logs are not arbitrary artifacts but purposeful markers developers employ to navigate complex code and runtime behaviors.

sentences.en: This paper presented the first large-scale empirical study of ad-hoc, or “printf-style,” logging by systematically mining accidental commits and analyzing live-streamed programming sessions.

By leveraging over 800,000 removed log statements across JavaScript, Java, and Python, as well as 36 hours of qualitative observations, we demonstrated that ad-hoc logs are not arbitrary artifacts but purposeful markers developers employ to navigate complex code and runtime behaviors.

blocks.html_en: Our findings highlight three themes. First, ad-hoc logs are disproportionately concentrated in contexts where reasoning about execution is especially difficult, such as asynchronous and callback functions in JavaScript or thread-related code in Java. Second, both ad-hoc and production logs tend to occur in functions with higher cyclomatic complexity. This shared pattern is consistent with logging serving as a means of observing runtime behavior in structurally complex functions, whether the logs address an immediate debugging need or remain for long-term production use. Third, developers refine ad-hoc logs iteratively, structure them with labels and formatting for clarity, and frequently remove them once their immediate purpose is served—though often with ad-hoc strategies for removal.

sentences.en: Our findings highlight three themes.

First, ad-hoc logs are disproportionately concentrated in contexts where reasoning about execution is especially difficult, such as asynchronous and callback functions in JavaScript or thread-related code in Java.
Second, both ad-hoc and production logs tend to occur in functions with higher cyclomatic complexity.

This shared pattern is consistent with logging serving as a means of observing runtime behavior in structurally complex functions, whether the logs address an immediate debugging need or remain for long-term production use.

Third, developers refine ad-hoc logs iteratively, structure them with labels and formatting for clarity, and frequently remove them once their immediate purpose is served—though often with ad-hoc strategies for removal.

blocks.html_en: Taken together, these results contribute both methodological and practical insights. Methodologically, our approach demonstrates how accidental artifacts in version control can serve as valuable data sources for understanding hidden aspects of software practice. Practically, our results suggest opportunities for tools that recommend effective logging locations, improve log readability, or visualize execution traces, thereby reducing the trial-and-error burden of printf debugging.

sentences.en: Taken together, these results contribute both methodological and practical insights.
Methodologically, our approach demonstrates how accidental artifacts in version control can serve as valuable data sources for understanding hidden aspects of software practice.

Practically, our results suggest opportunities for tools that recommend effective logging locations, improve log readability, or visualize execution traces, thereby reducing the trial-and-error burden of printf debugging.

blocks.html_en: Ultimately, ad-hoc logs, though ephemeral, offer a window into developers’ struggles and strategies for program comprehension through aggregation. By learning from these transient traces, researchers and tool builders can better support the everyday practices that shape debugging and development, bridging the gap between lightweight, local strategies and more formalized approaches to runtime understanding.
